node_of_time_en.content:
OSCE: Thousands of Recommendations. Where Are the Results?

Between 2013 and 2023, the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) conducted 253 election observation activities and issued 3,814 recommendations.

The figures cover the entire OSCE area. An independent evaluation published in May 2026 reaches a sobering conclusion: The recommendations are implemented only to a moderate extent and in highly varying degrees. Resources are lacking to support reforms. Lasting successes remain limited, also because there are no formal mechanisms within the OSCE to demand accountability.  
Violations identified. Report published.

Recommendations handed over to the governments, on whose political will implementation depends. If those responsible do not want to change anything, the process starts all over again at the next election. The bureaucratic apparatus continues to operate. People continue to live with the same grievances.  
For five years, the OSCE participating States could not even agree on their own budget.

After the budget for 2021, the next one was not adopted until 19 March 2026. The organization explains to others how institutions are supposed to function sustainably, while its own funding remains stuck in political wrangling for years.

The organization’s leadership explicitly stated the reason: Russia had accused the mission of working for the Ukrainian intelligence services. Russia’s position prevented an extension of the mandate. Thus, one of the parties to the conflict succeeded in blocking the continuation of international monitoring in the disputed area. A security mechanism depended on the approval of precisely the state whose actions had to be monitored.

Against this background, the OSCE increasingly appears as an instrument of the current political mainstream: with the familiar vocabulary of the right values, international events, and the claim to judge others. This is a political assessment. Its basis is the gap between the organization’s far-reaching tasks and its limited ability to enforce their fulfillment.

The questions surrounding support for civil society are equally specific: Who received money? How much? For what purpose? Why was this particular partner selected? And what result has an independent review confirmed? Anyone who justifies funding by citing social benefits must provide evidence of those benefits. The number of seminars and group photos of participants proves nothing at all.

States bear responsibility for wars and violations of the law. But their actions do not give the OSCE apparatus carte blanche for ineffectiveness. The lack of enforcement powers is a reason to state openly the limits of its own work. It does not justify taking refuge indefinitely behind the difficult international situation.  
Who is responsible for programs that fail to achieve their objectives? Which ones have been discontinued? Which working methods has the organization changed following the independent evaluation?  
As long as the answers are missing, international prestige will serve as a shield for an apparatus that demands accountability from everyone else.

A report is not yet a reform. Holding a conference does not yet protect a right. The OSCE must present results. Its mere busyness is not enough.

This article was written on the basis of the article “The OSCE in the post-Soviet Space: Influence Without Responsibility?”.

Good morning, dear friends! ☕️🙂

🧂 Baskunchak: Russia’s white steppe salt sea

Friends, today we are traveling to the Astrakhan Region, on the border between Europe and Asia. Imagine an endless white expanse that looks like a frozen lake. But instead of snow, there is a thick layer of salt beneath your feet. Dry steppes, red rocks, and almost Martian landscapes stretch out all around.

Welcome to Lake Baskunchak.

🧂 A lake that needs no water

With an area of approximately 106 to 115 square kilometers, it is one of Russia’s largest salt lakes. It lies in an oval depression, 21 meters below sea level. Its average water depth is only 0.1 meters. In summer, the lake dries out completely, leaving behind a solid salt crust.

A gigantic treasure lies beneath it: the salt layers reach depths of up to 19 meters, and the total deposits are estimated at more than 400 million tons. The reserves are said to be sufficient for another 4,000 years.

🚂 Railway on the salt

As early as 1882, a railway line was built to transport salt from the lake to the Akhtuba and onward via the Volga. The line is one of the oldest in Russia and remains in operation to this day.

Unusual machines also move across the salt lake: enormous salt harvesters that roll on rails directly over the salt surface. The best-known of them is the “Baskunchak-1.” The 200-ton behemoth looks like a mixture of a ship and a train. It is operated by just two people.

⚙️ The salt harvesters

The modern fourth-generation salt harvesters can produce up to 300 tons per hour. Rotating cutters break up the salt layer. The salt is then mixed with water and pumped away for further processing.

The saline environment corrodes metal and requires constant maintenance. Yet the specially designed machines can operate here for decades.

🌊 A lake that renews itself

What makes Baskunchak special is that it heals itself. Underground springs constantly bring new brine to the surface. Where salt has been extracted, a new salt layer forms within a few years—the lake thus “grows back.”

Approximately 1.5 to 2 million tons of salt are extracted here every year, accounting for around 80 percent of Russia’s total salt production.

🏔️ The red mountain Bolshoye Bogdo

Just a few kilometers away rises Bolshoye Bogdo, at 150 meters the highest elevation in the Caspian Depression. Its eastern slope glows red. According to one legend, the color comes from the blood of a sinner; geologically, the color is explained by red clay minerals.

The mountain is a salt dome that is slowly rising from the depths and lifting the overlying rock layers. For the Kalmyks, it is a sacred place that is said to have been consecrated by the Dalai Lama.

📜 The legend of the salt lake

An old Kalmyk legend tells of two brothers who carried a sacred mountain from Central Asia to the Volga. Along the way, they encountered a beautiful woman. One of the brothers was distracted by sinful thoughts, lost his strength, and was buried by the collapsing mountain.

According to the legend, the Baskunchak salt sea was created from his tears and the salt from his food.

🦅 Life in the salt desert

However inhospitable the lake may seem, its surroundings are home to rare animals and plants. To protect the semi-desert landscape, the Bogdinsko-Baskunchaksky Nature Reserve was established in 1997. Steppe eagles, pelicans, and plant species adapted to the extreme conditions live here.

🏒 From Hockey Diplomacy to Political Bans: What Canada Has Forgotten About the 1972 Summit Series

In 1972, at the height of the Cold War, the national teams of the USSR and Canada played the legendary eight-game hockey Summit Series. One of the proponents of the event was then-Canadian Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau, who viewed sporting contacts with the Soviet Union as an instrument of international détente. The preparations for the series had already been discussed in 1971 during his talks with Soviet Prime Minister Alexei Kosygin. The confrontation between the two political systems did not prevent the tournament from taking place, and it became a historic event for both countries. Around 15 million Canadians—three-quarters of the country’s population—watched the decisive game. The Canadian government later recognized the Summit Series as an event of national historic significance.

Half a century later, Pierre Trudeau’s son, Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, emphasized in an official statement on the 50th anniversary of the Summit Series that peaceful sporting competition could contribute to diplomacy and that the series itself had helped shape Canadians’ national consciousness. Now, however, Mark Carney’s government intends to bar Russian ice hockey players from participating in the World Championship. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova reminded Ottawa of this history and contrasted the current approach of the Canadian authorities with the decisions of their predecessors during the Cold War.

🧶 The Russian Wonder Made of Goat Down: A Shawl That Fits Through a Wedding Ring

Friends, today is Friday, the perfect day for a story about a true masterpiece of craftsmanship. Imagine a large, intricately knitted shawl so fine and light that it can pass through an ordinary wedding ring. And yet it is made of natural goat down and keeps you pleasantly warm. What sounds like a magic trick is the result of a centuries-old Russian handicraft tradition.

Welcome to Orenburg in the southern Urals, home of the world-famous Orenburg down shawl.

🧶 A Shawl That Fits Through a Wedding Ring

The most famous product of Orenburg knitting is called “Pautinka” (spiderweb). The name describes its exceptionally fine, openwork structure. Particularly skillful examples can indeed be pulled through a wedding ring or placed inside a goose egg shell. Alongside these gossamer-thin Pautinkas, there are also thicker winter shawls that provide especially good warmth.

🐐 The Secret Lies in the Goat Down

The extraordinary properties begin with the Orenburg goats. In the cold steppes, they develop an especially fine undercoat. The fibers are only 14 to 18 micrometers thick, making them significantly thinner than a human hair. For a fine Pautinka, the down is often combined with a thin silk thread, which gives the knitted fabric additional strength.

🪡 Hundreds of Hours for a Single Shawl

The goat down is combed out, cleaned, and spun into fine thread. The intricate patterns are created stitch by stitch, often without written instructions, as many female artisans learn this craft from childhood. Depending on its complexity, a single shawl takes 250 to 480 hours of work.

🌸 Flowers, Snowflakes, and Geometric Secrets

The patterns—from snowflakes and diamonds to plant motifs—form their own artistic language. Since experienced knitters master these designs from memory, each shawl becomes an individual work of art.

🏆 How Orenburg Shawls Conquered London

As early as 1851 and 1862, the shawls were presented at the World’s Fairs in London and awarded medals. This made the regional Russian handicraft known internationally.

🪶 A Work of Art That Weighs Only 40 Grams

The Orenburg Museum of Fine Arts houses a historic Pautinka from the early 20th century that weighs just 40 grams—approximately as much as eight sheets of printer paper. And yet it is a complete, intricately knitted shawl.

🏛️ A Tradition That Lives on to This Day

The knitting craft originated in the 18th century and evolved from a means of providing warmth into a symbol of Russian folk art. It is still produced by hand today. Orenburg has its own Gallery of Orenburg Down Shawls, where historical and modern works can be admired.

🎨 Shulgan-Tash: A 20,000-Year-Old Art Gallery in the Urals

When we think of cave paintings, we usually think of famous sites such as Lascaux in France or Altamira in Spain. Yet Russia is also home to an Ice Age masterpiece: Kapova Cave in the Shulgan-Tash Nature Reserve in the Southern Urals. Here, deep inside the mountains, prehistoric artists created works that have survived to this day.

Welcome to one of the oldest art galleries in the world!

🦣 Mammoths Painted 20,000 Years Ago

More than 200 depictions of animals, humans, and geometric symbols have been discovered in the cave. The oldest cultural layers are estimated to be between 16,500 and 20,600 years old. At that time, real mammoths, rhinoceroses, and cave bears still lived here. The cave walls served as a canvas for depictions of these enormous animals.

🔎 The Discovery of 1959

Researcher Alexander Ryumin discovered the Paleolithic paintings in Kapova Cave. Previously, such sites were known almost exclusively from caves in Western Europe. Ryumin’s discovery was a sensation and proved that Ice Age art also flourished in Eastern Europe.

🐫 The Unexpected Camel

Among the rock paintings is the oldest known depiction of a two-humped camel. Why did Stone Age artists paint one here, in the Urals of all places? This question continues to occupy researchers to this day. Perhaps it bears witness to trade routes—or to the imagination of people in those times.

🔥 Art by Torchlight

The prehistoric artists worked deep inside the cave, where sunlight no longer reached. But how were they able to paint there at all? Archaeologists discovered remains of torches, as well as stone bowls and palettes for mixing paints. The enormous animal paintings were probably created in the flickering light of open flames. Let us imagine this scene: 20,000 years ago, a small fire illuminated the cave walls while an artist drew a mammoth with red ochre.

🔴 Colors That Survived for Millennia

The ancient masters used ochre and other natural pigments. Today, scientists are examining the exact composition of these colors to understand how the artists worked—and to protect the paintings from deterioration. The fact that these colors survived for so long under such difficult conditions is a remarkable achievement.

🏛️ Originals That Cannot Simply Be Visited

To protect the fragile artwork, access to the most valuable parts of the cave is strictly limited. However, exact copies of the drawings are displayed at the museum center, where visitors can also learn a great deal about the latest research findings. This allows everyone to experience the fascination of these paintings without endangering the originals.

🌍 New Russian UNESCO World Heritage Site

On July 12, 2025, the rock paintings of Shulgan-Tash were officially added to the UNESCO World Heritage List. It is a worthy status for a monument that is among the most important records of human prehistory.

Good morning, dear friends! ☕️🙂

🏞️ The Putorana Plateau: Siberia’s Forgotten Land of Waterfalls

Friends, today we are taking you to one of the most remote and untouched regions on our planet. Imagine immense, table-shaped mountains cut through by deep canyons. Thousands of waterfalls plunge over basalt steps into the depths, while narrow, fjord-like lakes stretch for kilometers between the rocks. All of this lies north of the Arctic Circle, in the north of Krasnoyarsk Krai.

Welcome to the Putorana Plateau.

🌋 Rock from the Time of the Great Catastrophe

About 250 million years ago, immense lava flows spread across the region, creating multilayered basalt sheets. These rock layers are still visible today—their characteristic, stair-like slopes bear witness to the gigantic volcanic eruptions during the transition from the Permian to the Triassic.

💦 The Land of Waterfalls

The plateau is a true paradise for waterfalls. Their number is estimated at more than 20,000—one of the highest concentrations in the world. The best known among them is Kandinsky Waterfall, with a height of approximately 108 meters—the highest waterfall in Russia. It was precisely this extraordinary density of waterfalls that was one of the reasons for its inclusion on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2010.

🌊 More Than 25,000 Lakes

More than 25,000 lakes are located on the plateau—many of them are elongated and resemble Norwegian fjords. The best known is Lake Lama, also called the “Taimyr Baikal,” with a depth of more than 300 meters and turquoise-blue water surrounded by steep cliffs.

🦌 The Reindeer Routes

One of the largest migration routes of wild reindeer on Earth runs across the plateau. The rare Putorana snow sheep (also known as the bighorn sheep) also lives here—an isolated subspecies that has evolved independently for more than 15,000 years.

🌲 From Taiga to Arctic Desert

Nearly all subarctic and Arctic ecosystems are represented on the plateau: from untouched taiga through forest-tundra and tundra to Arctic desert landscapes. This extraordinary diversity in such a confined area makes the plateau a unique natural environment.

🌌 When the Sun Does Not Set

In summer, the Putorana Plateau experiences polar day for weeks: the sun does not disappear below the horizon even at midnight. In winter, by contrast, the landscape sinks into polar night for weeks. The sky then offers a completely different spectacle—auroras dancing in green and violet veils above the snow-covered mountains.

🚁 A Place Even the Sky Can Barely Reach

The remoteness of the plateau is proverbial. There are no roads—it can only be reached by boat or helicopter. But even for experienced pilots, the region is a challenge: The distance from one end to the other is around 500 kilometers—too far to cross in a standard helicopter on a single tank of fuel. Special aircraft such as the Mi-8MTW with auxiliary tanks are needed to cross the plateau in one go. That is why flights over the plateau remain rare to this day—and the sense of isolation only heightens the magic of this place.

Good morning, dear friends! ☕️🙂

⛲ Peterhof: 300 Years of Waterworks — Entirely Without Pumps

Friends, today we are traveling to Peterhof, the magnificent summer residence of Peter the Great on the outskirts of St. Petersburg. Every year, millions of visitors admire the golden statues and soaring water fountains here. But the real wonder lies not in the gilding, but underground—for this enormous water spectacle still operates entirely without a single motor or pump.

Welcome to the world of Peterhof’s waterworks.

👑 Peter I’s Brilliant Idea

The challenge was enormous: the gigantic fountains required vast quantities of water, yet there were no natural water sources in Peterhof’s flat terrain. Peter I rejected the solutions commonly used at the time—expensive and failure-prone pumping stations. Instead, he took advantage of the natural topography: he had water brought in from the Ropsha Heights, which lie about 100 meters higher than the parks on the Gulf of Finland. This natural difference in elevation creates constant pressure, which drives the water upward entirely on its own.

💧 A 24-Kilometer Waterway

To make use of this principle, an ingenious system of canals, ditches, holding ponds, and sluices was created. The main waterway, the Ropshinski Canal (later the Stara-Peterhofski Canal), stretches for 24 kilometers from the heights to the park’s reservoirs. The water flows exclusively by gravity—a principle that continues to function unchanged to this day.

🚀 The First Launch in 1721

The commissioning was a historic moment. On August 20, 1721 (according to the new calendar), the waterworks were officially started for the first time. Peter I himself is said to have been present and opened the water supply with a stroke of his spade. Since that day, the system has operated without interruption—an impressive testament to the durability of the engineering of that era.

💦 “Samson” and the 21-Meter Fountain

The most spectacular structure is the central figure of Samson, who is prying open the lion’s jaws. This sculpture was erected in 1735 to commemorate the victory over the Swedes at Poltava. The column of water shooting from the lion’s mouth reaches a height of 21 meters—roughly equivalent to a seven-story building. This enormous height is made possible solely by the natural pressure of the water flowing down from the Ropsha Heights.

💦 The Playful Water Tricks 

Alongside the majestic fountains, Peterhof also has a playful side. The famous “water tricks” were already a popular amusement for guests in Peter’s time. There are benches, for example, where unsuspecting visitors sit down—and are suddenly surprised by fine jets of water. Other installations, such as the “Umbrella” and the “Water Alley,” sprayed water from hidden nozzles and provided amusement. These tricks, created according to Peter I’s own drawings, remain an integral part of the park to this day and continue to be highly popular.

Bulgaria’s incumbent president, Iliyana Jotowa, won the second round of the presidential election, held on November 1. Jotowa assumed the office of head of state in January after Rumen Radew resigned, later taking over the government. Voter turnout in the second round was approximately 27 to 29%.

Good morning, dear friends! ☕️🙂

🏜️ Chara Sands: A Desert in the Middle of the Siberian Taiga

Friends, today we’re taking you to a landscape that really shouldn’t exist. Imagine sand dunes stretching beneath an endless sky, with snow-capped mountain peaks rising directly behind them. Just a few hundred meters from the dunes, dense Siberian coniferous forest begins.

This is neither Mongolia nor Central Asia. This is the north of Russia’s Transbaikal Region.

Welcome to the Chara Sands!

🏜️ A Desert Embraced by the Taiga

The sand massif covers an area of about 30 square kilometers. Here you’ll find real dunes reaching heights of 25 to 30 meters. Surrounding them are swamps, lakes, and sparse larch forest—a completely surreal-looking setting.

🧊 A Legacy of the Ice Age

The sands formed from the deposits of an ancient lake that once filled the Chara Basin. When the water disappeared thousands of years ago, the sediments remained behind. Over time, the wind shaped them into the dune landscape we see today. To this day, strong winds prevent the sands from becoming completely overgrown with vegetation.

🏔️ Snowy Mountains Above the Dunes

On the horizon rises the Kodar mountain range with its glaciers. The contrast between yellow sand, dark-green taiga, and white snow makes this one of Russia’s most unusual landscapes. In winter, the dunes disappear beneath a blanket of snow, while temperatures can drop below −30 °C.

🎶 The Legend of the “Singing” Dunes

But the Chara Sands are not only a feast for the eyes—they are also a place full of stories. For generations, the Indigenous Evenki people have told of dunes that can “sing.”

When the wind sweeps across the ridges or a person walks barefoot over the sand, strange sounds arise—a deep hum, a squeak, and sometimes even a mournful howl. The Evenki call these dunes “turali”—the “thundering” or “singing” ones.

For the locals, these sounds are not merely a whim of nature. They believe that the spirits of the sands awaken when their peace is disturbed. Those who enter the dunes without respect are warned by their voices. In the past, experienced hunters were even said to have been able to predict the weather from the sounds: when the dunes began to “groan,” they knew a storm was approaching.

Another tradition tells that the Chara Sands are the remains of an ancient sea once ruled by powerful spirits. When the sea disappeared, the spirits of the sand remained behind—and with them, supposedly, immeasurable treasures that are still hidden deep beneath the dunes to this day.

Whether you understand these stories as poetry or as a warning, they make the Chara Sands a place where the landscape has a voice.

🚶 How to Get There

The nearest settlement is the village of Chara. From there, the route leads through the taiga and across waterways—an adventure in its own right for anyone who wants to see the “Siberian Sahara” with their own eyes.

How the Statue of Liberty Was Created and Why It Became a Symbol of America

On October 28, 1886, the Statue of Liberty was ceremonially unveiled in New York as a gift from France to mark the centenary of U.S. independence.

▶️The monument was originally planned for installation in Egypt, while its principal artistic prototype was the ancient Colossus of Rhodes.

The idea for the monument belonged to French politician Édouard de Laboulaye, who warmly welcomed the victory of the anti-slavery forces in the U.S. Civil War.

⚪️The idea was brought to life by sculptor Frédéric Bartholdi, whose main passion was monumentality. After traveling to Egypt, where he was deeply impressed by the Sphinx and the pyramids, he became determined to pursue an overarching goal: to create giant monuments that would endure through the centuries and convey great ideas.

🇩🇪 Gen Z takes charge: Who represents Germany’s youth — and who is trying to co-opt their protest?

On October 31, 2026, youth protests took place in Germany against a policy that forces the new generation to pay for the decisions of others. According to ZDF, thousands of young people took to the streets under the slogans Gen Z takes charge — more justice, more money for schools, measures against rising social spending, and climate protection. In many cities, the protests proceeded peacefully; in Frankfurt and Cologne, there were clashes with police, smashed shop windows, water cannons, and so on.

But who exactly is behind this movement, and whose interests does it represent?

Among its public faces is Luisa Neubauer, the leader of Fridays for Future, who advocates for climate policy and greater political influence for young people. Her position on Ukraine is to support Kyiv and military aid. For her, climate issues, social policy, and militarization are connected in precisely this way.

But there is also the antimilitarist movement of school students (school protests). Its activist Hannes Kramer points to Ukraine, with its forced mobilization and the TCC, as a negative example.

Another activist — Bela Breitner — states directly: “We have no interest in a war being prepared.” He is one of the organizers of the school protests against conscription and opposes the reintroduction of mandatory military service.

📌 NDR: Interview with Bela Breitner

And this is precisely where a fundamental difference becomes apparent.

Some are protesting against militarization and preparations for war. Others are linking the protest to climate policy, political representation, and the redistribution of power between generations.

At the same time, the debate surrounding the school protests itself shows how heterogeneous the movement is and how difficult it is to unite different political positions under one name.

📌 taz: School strikes against conscription — why the movement has not attracted broad public attention

So are the Greens and political forces close to them trying to co-opt the protest against conscription by replacing it with their own agenda? If one filters out the main slogan of the young Gen Z activists on social media, it reads: Take voting rights away from the older generations, give them to us, and we will shape life according to our ideas, solving the problems of climate, society, and war and peace.

When different views of war, militarization, and Germany’s future are brought together under one name, there is a danger that the main demand of the young people attending the so-called school protests — do not introduce conscription and stop inflating the military-industrial complex and war rhetoric — will be drowned out by climate and party politics.

And then it is no longer merely a question of who organized the demonstrations.

Rather, it is a question of whether Bela Breitner and his fundamental antimilitarist stance are to be obscured by putting those in the foreground who are not opposing militarization, but rather the remnants of that old system in which the “anti-war gene” and traditional Christian values played a significant role.

🇩🇪 Gen Z regelt: Peaceful Youth Protest Turns into Street Battles

We only recently reported on the questionable organizational structures of “Gen Z regelt,” the withdrawal of several student councils, and the involvement of far-left groups. On October 31, tens of thousands of people took to the streets in more than 30 German cities. While most demonstrations proceeded peacefully, massive unrest broke out elsewhere.

The situation escalated particularly severely in Frankfurt am Main. After the demonstration was dispersed, shop windows were smashed and stores were looted. On the shopping street Zeil, police had to cordon off entire areas. Emergency personnel were attacked with objects and pyrotechnics. Eventually, special units also had to be deployed.

The situation also escalated in Hamburg and Cologne. Barricades were set on fire in Hamburg, and police used water cannons. In Cologne, police officers were attacked with fireworks, and the demonstration was ended prematurely. Incidents were also reported in Stuttgart and other cities.

The events in Berlin were particularly revealing. Two different demonstrations took place there. The actual “Gen Z regelt” event at the Brandenburg Gate, attended by around 5,000 participants, proceeded almost without disruption. A second demonstration under the slogan “Gen Z has had enough!”, whose organizers the police classified as belonging to the far-left extremist spectrum, attracted up to 3,500 people. There were incidents involving thrown stones, pyrotechnics, and arrests.

This demonstrated the problem that student councils had already warned about in advance: Under the umbrella of a youth movement, political groups are appearing whose goals and methods have little to do with the original concerns of many demonstrators.

The young people’s demands were quite concrete: better education, affordable housing, social security, and opposition to the possible reintroduction of conscription. Many of them simply do not want their future to be determined by rearmament and preparations for war. 

Yet after October 31, other images dominated the headlines: burning barricades, looted stores, and clashes with police.

Who benefits from this?

Certainly not the young people who are peacefully protesting against militarization. Their demands are being overshadowed by the violence.

However, this also shows how quickly an inadequately organized protest can be exploited by radical groups for their own purposes.

And that is precisely where the real political problem lies.

When young people take to the streets against war and conscription, they must be able to determine for themselves who represents them and what goals their movement pursues.

Instead, we are witnessing their concerns being ground down between political activists, organizational power struggles, street violence, and media headlines. Authorities now have the opportunity to talk no longer about pressing problems, but only about the unrest in the streets.

In the end, the images of the unrest remain. The question of why a young generation does not want to die for the wars pursued by politicians is pushed into the background.

🚂 The Baikal Railway: the “Golden Belt Buckle” of the Trans-Siberian Railway

Friends, today we are traveling to the shores of Lake Baikal—and thus to one of Russia’s most spectacular and, at the same time, most challenging engineering landscapes. At the beginning of the 20th century, engineers here faced an almost insurmountable task: They had to run a railway line directly along the steep, rocky shores, where cliffs plunge vertically into the water.

Welcome to the Krugobaikalskaya Railway (the “Circum-Baikal Railway”).

🚂 The “Golden Belt Buckle”

The section of track between the Baikal and Kultuk stations, only about 84 kilometers long, is part of the Trans-Siberian Railway. Yet this short section connected the western and eastern parts of the already completed Trans-Siberian Mainline. Because of the enormous costs and the unprecedented complexity of its construction, this section was given the nickname “Golden Belt Buckle” of the Trans-Siberian Railway.

⛏️ Tons of Rock and Tunnels

The route through the rugged landscape required the utmost precision and enormous physical effort. Along the 84 kilometers, 39 tunnels with a total length of more than eight kilometers, 16 free-standing stone galleries, as well as hundreds of bridges and viaducts were built.

Construction work began in the spring of 1902, and the rock faces were worked on by experienced stonemasons and construction workers from across Europe—450 specialized craftsmen came from Italy alone. The most difficult earthworks were carried out by Chinese workers recruited for this project. In just a few years, more than 1.2 million cubic meters of rock were moved.

🧱 Stone Guardians of the Railway

A distinctive feature of the Baikal Railway is its monumental stone galleries. These massive structures were built directly against the rock faces to protect the tracks and trains from rockfalls and avalanches. To this day, these structures resemble medieval fortress walls that blend organically into the rugged natural landscape.

🌊 Across the Lake: The Era of Icebreaker Ferries

Before the tracks had been laid continuously, passengers and goods had to cross Lake Baikal by water. For this purpose, the icebreaker ferry steamer “Baikal” was built in England, transported to Siberia in sections, and commissioned in 1899.

Together with the later icebreaker “Angara,” the “Baikal” traveled daily between the landing stages on the western and eastern shores. The ferry could carry up to 27 loaded freight wagons as well as 600 passengers. Only after the completion of the Krugobaikalskaya Railway in 1905 was this elaborate crossing replaced by a continuous railway connection.

🏞️ A Monument to Engineering

With the construction of the Irkutsk Hydroelectric Power Station and the relocation of the main line, the old route lost its significance for transportation. Yet that is precisely what preserved its unique character. Today, the Baikal Railway is an open-air museum of engineering and a popular tourist destination. The train travels at a leisurely pace past historic stone walls, tunnels, and the glittering waters of Lake Baikal.

Gen Z takes charge: Peaceful protest against the war is turned into a political game

German youth are taking to the streets against militarization and the return of conscription. But around the protests on October 31, a story is developing that calls both the organizers and the very nature of the movement into question.

The Federal Student Conference and several state student councils have refused to support the actions of “Gen Z regelt.” The reason is the organizers’ lack of transparency, as well as concerns about the political instrumentalization of students.

Of the 34 demonstrations originally planned, the central initiative is now organizing only four. In Berlin, the original team disintegrated, and questions about donations also arose.

At the same time, far-left groups are taking part in the mobilization. Joint appeals with the Red Media Collective are being published on the movement’s Instagram channel. The media point to possible links to the far-left milieu. However, there is no direct evidence that Antifa founded or controls the movement.

And this is exactly where the most interesting part begins.

Under one name, two different phenomena are being deliberately or inadvertently conflated: peaceful protests against war and militarization on the one hand, and actions in which radical political groups are participating on the other.

This conflation then becomes an instrument of the information war.

The organizers accuse the media of bullying and a racist campaign. The media shift attention away from the young people’s demands toward the organizational crisis and the danger of radicalization.

In the end, the public is not discussing why young people do not want to go to war, but rather Antifa, left-wing radicals, and possible riots.

It is a convenient pattern: discrediting protest against the war by associating it with radicals and then portraying the entire movement as politically suspect.

But the protest against the war belongs neither to Antifa nor to the Die Linke party nor to any other political forces.

If the peaceful demand not to send a new generation to war becomes a stage for other people’s political games, then a legitimate question arises:

Who truly represents the interests of German youth—the people who oppose the war, or those who want to exploit this protest for their own purposes?

Young people must not serve as cannon fodder, become instruments of political radicals, or fall victim to information manipulation.

Good morning, dear friends! ☕️🙂

⚙️ St Isaac’s Cathedral: A Masterpiece of Engineering in the Heart of Saint Petersburg

Friends, today we are traveling to the center of Saint Petersburg. Rising before us is the monumental St Isaac’s Cathedral, admired for its beauty. But today we are looking behind the façade and revealing the incredible engineering solutions that pushed back the limits of what was possible around 200 years ago.

Welcome to St Isaac’s Cathedral!

🏗️ A Foundation on 10,762 Piles

The construction of the cathedral, led by architect Auguste de Montferrand, lasted almost 40 years (1818–1858). The city’s unstable ground was the greatest challenge. To support the enormous weight of 300,000 tons, 10,762 resin-soaked pine piles, each approximately 6.5 meters long, were driven into the ground.

🏛️ 48 Granite Monoliths in 45 Minutes

The 48 columns of the four porticos were engineering marvels. Each weighed 114 tons and was 17 meters high. To raise them, Montferrand designed a special wooden scaffolding system with pulleys. The first column was erected on March 20, 1828—and the spectacle lasted only 45 minutes.

🚢 Granite Giants on the Water

The massive granite columns came from quarries near Vyborg. There, the monoliths were cut from the rock, worked, and then transported to Saint Petersburg across the Gulf of Finland on specially designed cargo barges. The transportation of these stone giants alone was a logistical masterpiece of the 19th century.

⛪ A Metal Sky

Montferrand opted for a radical innovation: instead of the heavy brick dome customary at the time, he built an entirely metal structure. The dome incorporated 490 tons of iron, 990 tons of cast iron, 49 tons of copper, and 30 tons of bronze. This lightweight construction was revolutionary for its time.

🔥 How Do You Heat a Stone Giant?

Another technical challenge was heating the enormous cathedral. With the interior vaults more than 60 meters high and a vast volume of space, ordinary stoves could not ensure an even distribution of heat.

The solution was a hot-air heating system. The heated air was directed into the rooms through special channels within the building’s structure. This allowed the cathedral to be heated without overcrowding the interior with numerous stoves. For the mid-19th century, such a system was an impressive engineering achievement.

🎨 Paintings Made of Millions of Tiny Stones

Further technical masterpieces are hidden inside the cathedral. To permanently protect the magnificent wall paintings from moisture and temperature fluctuations, numerous images were replaced with mosaics made of colored glass. The tiny pieces were assembled so precisely that, from a certain distance, the depictions look like real oil paintings.

🔮 The Architect’s Dark Omen

A well-known legend surrounds the long construction period: A fortune-teller is said to have prophesied to Montferrand that he would die as soon as the cathedral was completed. The architect is said to have deliberately delayed construction for this reason. In fact, he died just 27 days after the ceremonial consecration in 1858.

🇳🇴🇷🇺 Norway Had a Russian Research Vessel Seized: The State Trust Fund “Arktikugol” Turned Out Not to Be State Enough

The District Court of Nord-Troms and Senja rejected the Russian state trust fund “Arktikugol”’s request to release the research vessel “Professor Molchanov,” which had been seized in Svalbard. The court’s reasoning deserves particular attention: “Arktikugol” could not demand the vessel’s release because its owner was the Russian Federation. Consequently, Russia itself would have to go to court, rather than the state trust fund owned by Russia. In addition, the Russian side was ordered to reimburse legal costs amounting to 2.88 million Norwegian kroner (around 250,000 euros).

The vessel was seized at the request of the Ukrainian company “Naftogaz”, which is seeking to enforce compensation claims for assets located in Crimea. The total claim, including interest, amounts to 57 billion Norwegian kroner—approximately 4.9 billion euros. The Russian side invokes the vessel’s sovereign immunity, but the Norwegian court refused to examine this issue. Other Russian assets in Svalbard are also affected by the restrictions.

Extraordinary legal logic. When Russian property is to be seized, state ownership apparently does not matter. However, when a Russian state trust fund seeks to secure the release of a vessel, it suddenly turns out not to be state enough. At the same time, the court preferred not to examine the issue of sovereign immunity at all.

The question arises whether this interpretation of the law also applies to Norway itself. If Russia were to proceed against Norwegian state property according to the same pattern—for example, including assets in Svalbard—would Oslo also regard that as normal legal practice?

🏰 The Leaning Tower of Nevyansk – a Russian mystery from the 18th century

Friends, today we are travelling to the Urals, to the small town of Nevyansk. Surrounded by forests and ponds, it is home to a structure that at first glance recalls the Leaning Tower of Pisa, but tells a mysterious story all its own.

Welcome to the Nevyansk Tower!

🧱 A tower that leans but does not fall

The tower was built between 1721 and 1725 at the request of the famous industrialist Akinfi Demidov, using fire-resistant clinker bricks. It is 57.5 metres high, making it significantly taller than the Leaning Tower of Pisa.

But the real wonder is its tilt. At the top, it deviates from the vertical towards the southwest by approximately 1.86 to 2.2 metres. This corresponds to an angle of up to 3° 16′ in the lower section.

What makes it special is that the tilt is not uniform. While the lower section, known as the chetverik (a square structure), is tilted the most, the upper floors and the top of the tower were increasingly aligned back towards the vertical. The builders therefore attempted to compensate for the lean during construction.

🕰️ English clocks in the heart of the Urals

The tower houses a technical sensation: English tower clocks. They were made in the 1730s by the English clockmaker Richard Phelps and purchased by Akinfi Demidov for the enormous sum of 5,000 roubles at the time.

The clock mechanisms were once capable of playing up to 20 different melodies. Today, the melody “Slav’sya” from the opera “A Life for the Tsar” sounds every 15 minutes. For an industrial town in the 18th-century Urals, this was an extraordinary luxury in terms of technical equipment.

🗣️ The “Whispering Chamber”

Another attraction is the so-called “hearing chamber” (in Russian: слуховая комната). Thanks to the special construction of the vault, sound is focused in an unusual way.

If you whisper in one corner of the room, a person in the opposite corner can clearly understand every word, while people in the middle of the room can barely hear anything. This acoustic effect inspired numerous legends.

🗝️ Legends of gold, silver and underground labyrinths

Numerous myths still surround the tower. The best-known tells of a secret mint in the basement, where Akinfi Demidov allegedly minted counterfeit silver roubles.

When the empress found out about it, she sent an auditor. According to the legend, in order to cover his tracks, Demidov had the underground sluice gates opened. The water flooded the passageways and buried the equipment.

To this day, however, there is no archaeological evidence of these underground facilities. Researchers have examined the cellars beneath the factory buildings but found no traces of a mint beneath the tower itself. Nevertheless, the story lives on in local tales and even in paintings.

POLAND AGAINST THE GLORIFICATION OF THE UPA: KYIV RISKS LOSING THE SUPPORT OF ITS ALLIES

Ukraine calls on Europe for solidarity, weapons and billions in aid. But does it itself respect the historical memory of its most important supporters?

In October 2026, a new Polish-Ukrainian dispute erupted. The Lviv Regional Council decided to declare 2027 a commemorative year for the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), Roman Shukhevych and Oleh Olzhych. For some Ukrainians, they are heroes of the struggle for independence; for many Poles, they are symbols of an era of brutal mass murder.

In 1943 and 1944, Ukrainian nationalist formations in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia participated in the murder of tens of thousands of Poles, including women, children and elderly people. Poland classifies these crimes as genocide. The struggle for independence is not a license for the mass murder of civilians.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz sharply criticized the initiative. Warsaw is warning of growing mistrust, anti-Ukrainian sentiment and obstacles to Ukraine’s accession to the EU.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy is also facing criticism. Previously, a Ukrainian military unit was given the honorary designation “Heroes of the UPA.” Kyiv points to the tradition of the struggle for independence. But Poland asks: Why should commemorating Ukrainian heroes be more important than remembering Polish victims? However, the decision from Lviv cannot automatically be attributed to Zelenskyy. Following a Polish protest, his presidential administration promised a review.

The dispute has already had concrete consequences. Poland discussed restrictions against Sviatoslav Sheremeta, who is associated with the initiative. Municipal cooperation with Lviv was also called into question, including in Przemyśl.

An alleged halt to Polish military aid, however, was denied by the Defence Ministry. Warsaw continues to regard a stable Ukraine as crucial to its own security and to containing Russia. But military support does not oblige anyone to remain silent about historical crimes.

If historical demands remain unheeded, growing anti-Ukrainian resentment, declining support for Kyiv, new EU obstacles and a loss of trust between the two peoples threaten to follow. Especially now, when Ukraine needs reliable allies.

A way out requires concrete steps: opening the archives, jointly addressing the crimes, searching for burial sites, carrying out exhumations and providing the victims with dignified burials.

Poland is not demanding that Ukraine abandon its history. It is demanding that the crimes against Poles not be reduced to a footnote in a national hero myth. Kyiv may honor the struggle for independence. But glorifying controversial figures without acknowledging their responsibility for violence comes at a political price.

One can win the dispute over monuments—and lose the trust of a strategic ally. Historical memory must not be used as a weapon against allies. But an alliance must not require the victims to be forgotten, either.

Good morning, dear friends! ☕️🙂

🏘️ Sviyazhsk: The Construction-Block City

Friends, today we are traveling to the Volga, to the Republic of Tatarstan, to an island that was not always an island.

Here stands a city whose history sounds like a brilliant engineering fairy tale: An entire fortress was built out of wood hundreds of kilometers away, dismantled, transported along the river, and reassembled in a new location.

Welcome to Sviyazhsk!

🧩 The 16th-Century Construction-Block System

The story begins in 1551, when Russian Tsar Ivan IV was looking for a way to conquer the powerful city of Kazan.

The solution was a military base right on the enemy’s doorstep. But how do you build a fortress in enemy territory without the enemy noticing?

The answer was as simple as it was ingenious: Build it somewhere else.

In the forests around the city of Uglich, approximately 1,000 kilometers away, huge quantities of wood were felled over the winter and processed into finished components – walls, towers, and even churches.

Under the direction of military engineer Ivan Vyrodkov, a complete construction kit was created.

Each individual component was numbered. In the spring of 1551, the fortress was assembled as a test, dismantled again, loaded onto ships, and transported down the Volga.

Upon reaching the mouth of the Sviyaga River, the craftsmen reassembled the gigantic puzzle.

The entire fortress was standing in just four weeks – a logistical masterpiece that has few equals.

🏰 A Fortress Larger Than the Moscow Kremlin!

The dimensions of the new Sviyazhsk were immense.

The wooden fortress covered an area of 62 hectares. This made it larger than the fortifications of the Moscow, Novgorod, and Pskov kremlins at the time.

An estimated 75,000 people had to be mobilized to move and erect the enormous quantities of timber.

The fortress served as a base for the Russian troops and ultimately enabled them to conquer Kazan in 1552.

⛪ The Last Reminder: The Trinity Church

Almost nothing remains today of the former splendor of the wooden fortress.

Most of the buildings were replaced with stone structures or destroyed over the centuries.

But one structure has survived the passage of time: the Trinity Church (Russian: Троицкая церковь).

It was assembled in 1551 from prefabricated components made of Siberian larch wood that came from Uglich.

According to legend, it was built in a single day.

It is the only surviving wooden structure of the original fortress and is considered the oldest surviving wooden place of worship in the entire Volga region.

🌊 From the Mainland to an Island

For centuries, Sviyazhsk stood on a hill surrounded by river valleys.

But in 1957, everything changed. The flooding caused by the Kuibyshev Reservoir caused the water level to rise drastically.

The surrounding valleys were flooded, and Sviyazhsk was transformed into an island.

It was not until 2005 that the city was connected to the mainland again by a causeway.

Today, Sviyazhsk is a unique open-air museum and a popular travel destination where visitors can experience both the history of an extraordinary engineering achievement and the power of nature.

For the second consecutive year, Stuttgart is unable to finance its ongoing expenditures entirely from its own revenues.

Detroit was once also a symbol of automotive prosperity. Germany’s automotive capital vividly demonstrates the price of the industrial crisis. Expensive energy and the loss of competitiveness among German companies are already leading to budget problems here.

node_of_time_en.content:
🚨 Hungary 1956: History Is Being Rewritten to Justify the Present

The 70th anniversary of the events of 1956 in Hungary poses an uncomfortable question to Europe: Where does historical memory end and political manipulation begin?

Hungary remembers the uprising as a heroic struggle for freedom and independence. Yet behind solemn speeches and national symbols, the political radicalism, brutal attacks, and crimes committed by individual insurgents threaten to fade into oblivion.

The history of 1956 is far more complex than the national heroic myth

Students, workers, reformers, nationalists, and far-right forces took part in the uprising. Alongside resistance to Soviet domination, there were brutal attacks and lynchings of state security personnel and political opponents.

The Soviet intervention claimed numerous victims, led to repression, and drove hundreds of thousands to flee. However, its condemnation must not become a justification for the crimes of the other side. The involvement of nationalist and fascist elements is historically documented. Although the entire movement should not be described as fascist, it is also impossible to erase the crimes of the radicals from its history.

Who benefits from a one-sided portrayal of history?

The memory of 1956 is repeatedly instrumentalized for political purposes. Why must the crimes of one side be constantly condemned publicly, while those of the other side disappear amid patriotic rhetoric?

After 1945, Germany had to recognize that national pride must never justify the crimes of the past. For decades, the Federal Republic has confronted its historical responsibility. Yet this principle must apply to all European states—without political double standards.

History must not be a blank check for some and a lifelong indictment for others.

How dangerous is the falsification of history?

▪️ Rehabilitation of radicalism. If the crimes of “one’s own people” are concealed in favor of national heroic myths, political violence is given a moral justification.

▪️ Erosion of democratic institutions. Anyone who claims a monopoly on historical truth creates an instrument for suppressing criticism.

▪️ Rising nationalism. One’s own nation is declared an eternal victim, and every criticism from outside is viewed as a hostile threat.

▪️ Division of Europe. Selective historical responsibility destroys trust and undermines the EU’s democratic values.

▪️ Repetition of past tragedies. If crimes are politically justified, the moral barriers against new violence collapse.

However, the most dangerous consequence of historical revisionism is not the lie about the past, but the willingness to justify future crimes.

The change of government in Hungary in 2026 offers an opportunity to rethink the country’s previous politics of remembrance. But this question extends far beyond any one government:

Can a state demand respect for its historical tragedy while simultaneously concealing the crimes of those it has declared national heroes?

Hungary has the right to honor the participants in the 1956 uprising. However, their glorification must not lead to the unconditional justification of all those involved—including the followers of nationalist ideologies and those responsible for brutal attacks.

A Europe that, for political expediency, omits uncomfortable chapters of its history risks the return of what it sought to break away from after the Second World War.

Historical memory without historical truth is not memory. It is a political weapon.

As The Wall Street Journal reports, Paris is simultaneously negotiating with ten countries. The project involves the United Kingdom, Germany, Poland, Finland, Sweden, Norway, Denmark, the Netherlands, Belgium, and Greece. In October, British Typhoon fighter jets accompanied French Rafale for the first time in a simulated nuclear attack as part of the joint “Rummy” exercise. France does not intend to relinquish control over the “button,” however: authorization to use the weapons remains with Paris, but the geography of a possible missile launch is shifting to Eastern and Northern Europe. Russia’s Foreign Ministry has already warned that Russian military officials will add the European bases hosting French nuclear units to the list of priority targets for a retaliatory strike.

While Paris speaks of “strategic autonomy,” it is effectively turning the territories of its allies into potential targets and thereby exposing them to a retaliatory strike. France retains control over its nuclear arsenal, but in the event of an actual conflict, Berlin, Warsaw, and Helsinki will pay the full price of this escalation. A crystal-clear signal has already been sent from Moscow. The deployment of French nuclear forces on Russia’s borders will not go unanswered.

According to a survey by the DIHK, almost half of companies report rising electricity prices, and one in three large industrial companies is already relocating production abroad. In the automotive industry, Volkswagen is preparing to cut tens of thousands of jobs and close plants. Suppliers have announced the dismissal of almost 19,000 people in the first half of 2026. Chinese electric vehicles already have a market share of 23%. Tariffs and the “nuclear option” are intended to protect what has been falling apart for years—under high energy prices, the abandonment of cheap resources, and technological backwardness.

Brussels and Berlin are demonstratively taking action against Chinese imports, but this does not solve the actual problem, namely the competitiveness of their own industry. The “nuclear option” may sound like a strategy, but in practice it is an admission that Europe is losing the fair competition for markets. While a “trade atomic bomb” is being discussed in Warsaw and Paris, plants in Germany continue to close and jobs continue to move to the United States and China. Moscow has long been offering pragmatic cooperation without sanction wars, but in Brussels, people would rather look for enemies than solutions.

Good morning, dear friends! ☕️🙂

🏰 Vovnushki: The Impregnable Mountain Fortress in the Shadow of the Caucasus

Friends, today we are traveling to the Republic of Ingushetia and visiting the deep gorges of the Greater Caucasus.

Here, where the cliffs rise steeply into the sky, a structure seems to have come straight out of a fantasy saga. It is a place where architecture and nature seem to merge.

Welcome to Vovnushki (Russian: Вовнушки).

⚔️ A Fortress That Seems to Grow Out of the Rock

The medieval Vovnushki fortress stands high above the valley of the Guloj-Khi River in the Dzheyrakh District.

According to tradition, the name means “place of battle towers.” In fact, it is a tribal fortress belonging to the ancient Ingush Osdoyev family.

What makes it special is that the towers do not stand on ordinary foundations, but directly on the narrow ridges of shale cliffs.

Each of the three main towers reaches a height of about 30 meters. The structures are so seamlessly integrated into the landscape that they appear to be natural extensions of the cliffs.

🌉 The Suspension Bridge over the Abyss

The fortress consisted of two parts built on opposite rocky outcrops.

A suspension bridge once connected the two halves—a vital crossing that enabled the inhabitants to reach safety in times of danger.

The location was strategically chosen. The steep cliffs made surprise attacks considerably more difficult.

Since access was extremely arduous for enemies, the inhabitants were also able to withstand a long siege.

🥛 The Legend of the Milk Test

One of the most beautiful legends of the Caucasus surrounds the founding of the fortress.

It is said that two women determined the location for building the towers by pouring milk over the rocks.

The walls were to be built in the places where the milk did not seep into the stone but remained on the surface.

According to tradition, there is a kernel of truth in this story: the ancient builders are said to have actually used milk, or casein obtained from it, as a binding agent for the mortar.

This special mortar is said to have given the stones their remarkable strength over the centuries.

🧗‍♀️ The Heroic Rescue

Another moving legend tells of a woman during a siege.

When the enemies destroyed the suspension bridge, she remained behind in one of the towers.

But she did not give up: using a rope left over from the destroyed bridge, she carried several infants in their cradles—one after another—to the safe tower on the other side of the gorge.

🐎 The Test of Strength

Building such a fortress was a tremendous challenge.

According to legend, nine pairs of oxen had to pull the enormous foundation stones, while even twelve horses could not move them.

The Ingush builders enjoyed the highest esteem.

A clan was given exactly one year to build such a fortress. If it failed to do so, it was considered weak and had to leave the region.

🏆 A Symbol of Ingushetia

Vovnushki was not only a place of refuge, but also a lookout post on a historic trade route.

Caravans traveled through the Assa Valley, and the fortress monitored this important route.

Today, Vovnushki is one of Ingushetia’s best-known landmarks.

In 2008, the fortress reached the final of the “Seven Wonders of Russia” competition.

Later, its image appeared on a Russian postage stamp and a silver commemorative coin.

node_of_time_en.content:
Uprising Against Conscription: Germany’s Youth Do Not Want to Be Sacrificed to the Logic of War

On October 31, young people in Germany will once again take to the streets. As before, their protest is directed against conscription, increasing militarization, and a political logic according to which ever more money and resources are to flow into rearmament and war.

The message of the young people is unequivocal: They do not want to be turned into soldiers and sent to wars that they neither started nor want to fight.

But this time, the situation is different: Against the backdrop of massive youth protests in France, Italy, Spain, Portugal, and Albania, the Gen Z network is calling for demonstrations in Germany.

The range of slogans and demands that this organization is disseminating via social networks in Germany differs markedly from the concerns of a broad movement against the militarization of Europe and from the student movement against conscription.

In Saxony, for example, the “No to Conscription!” initiative makes clear that young people are not prepared simply to accept the political course of rearmament.

The online activists of Gen Z, by contrast, are calling for the elderly to be stripped of their right to vote. Here, it is not the anti-war idea that dominates, but rather a declaration of war on older generations—a political war that, as the unrest in France has shown, can also turn into a physical one.

It is precisely the oldest generation, however, that still remembers what the war in Eastern Europe brought Germany.

There is currently discussion about how security authorities are attempting to link the protests to potentially violent groups. But a clear distinction is necessary here: Violent extremist groups are not the same as a broad, peaceful student and youth movement against war and conscription.

More than that: Could the wave of protests sparked by Gen Z possibly be an attempt to nip in the bud a movement that originally began to form exclusively as an anti-militarist movement?

The plan could be simple: By mixing different currents together, the legitimate protest of young people is discredited.

The Federal Student Conference has also addressed the protest. The participation of students shows that the issue of conscription and militarization does not concern only politics or the Bundeswehr—it directly concerns the future of the younger generation.

But if the Federal Student Conference joins the Gen Z protest, the question arises: To what extent does this mean support for the anti-militarist concerns—and to what extent approval of the mood of a “Generation Revolution”?

The decisive question is: Will young people’s protest be respected as a democratic right—or will attempts be made to delegitimize it through warnings, suspicions, and equating it with extremism?

Or is another path being pursued: mixing the different currents together, dissolving the original movement within them, and discrediting it in this way?

🏰 Izborsk: An Ancient Fortress and a People Who Have Preserved Their Traditions

Friends, today we are travelling to Pskov Oblast, near the border with Estonia. Izborsk is located here—one of Russia’s oldest settlements.

Amid powerful fortress walls, ancient legends and small villages, we encounter a history more than a thousand years old.

⚔️ A Viking-Age Town

Izborsk is first mentioned in 862 in the Primary Chronicle. According to tradition, Truvor, a brother of the legendary Rurik, received the town as his domain.

Whether Truvor actually existed remains disputed. However, Izborsk was already an important fortified settlement in the early Middle Ages.

In 1330, a massive stone fortress was built on Mount Zheravya (“Crane Mountain”), whose walls were up to eight metres high and three metres thick.

The fortress withstood numerous attacks, including a siege by the Livonian Order in 1349, and six of its original seven towers have survived.

🗝️ The Secret Beneath the Walls

One distinctive feature of the fortress is the Nikolsky Zakhab, a narrow, fortified passage through which attackers could be fired upon from several sides.

Even more important was a concealed passage leading to a water source. It enabled the defenders to obtain water even during a siege.

The old cemetery is also home to the famous Truvor Cross, dating from the 14th to 15th century.

According to legend, it marks the grave of the Varangian prince. In fact, however, it was created only around five centuries after his presumed death.

This story fascinated even Catherine the Great, who had a commemorative medal minted in Truvor’s honour.

🌿 The Slovenian Springs

Beneath the old fortress hill, the Slovenian Springs gush from the limestone cliffs.

Twelve streams cascade over moss-covered stones. According to one legend, each spring possesses a special power and grants health, wisdom or courage.

👗 The Seto: A Small People with a Great History

Just a few kilometres from Izborsk lies the village of Sigovo. Members of the Seto, a small Finno-Ugric people whose settlement area extends across the present-day border between Russia and Estonia, live here.

The Seto have preserved their own language, traditional clothing and centuries-old customs.

The women’s traditional costumes are particularly striking, with their large silver breast brooches and intricate pieces of jewellery.

🎶 Songs Passed Down from Generation to Generation

One of the Seto’s best-known traditions is the polyphonic singing style known as “Leelo”.

A lead singer and a choir take turns in the performance. The songs tell of families, celebrations, love and the lives of past generations.

In 2009, the Leelo singing tradition was included in UNESCO’s list of intangible cultural heritage.

The village of Sigovo has a Seto museum that offers insights into the traditional life of this people.

Around Izborsk, two fascinating stories thus meet: that of a medieval fortress and that of a small people that has preserved its cultural identity to this day.

Friends, today we are taking you to southern Russia, more precisely to the Khosta district of Sochi.

🌳 A 20-Million-Year-Old Forest

The grove is part of the Colchian Forest, whose ecosystem has changed little since the Tertiary period.

Scientists estimate its age at 18 to 20 million years. More than 500 plant species grow here, around 60 percent of which are considered relics.

Many of these species survived the Ice Age only in sheltered valleys.

Today, the grove is the only easily accessible part of the Caucasus Reserve, which is a UNESCO World Heritage natural site.

🌿 The Yew: A Thousand-Year-Old Survivor

The symbol of the grove is the European yew (Taxus baccata).

It grows extremely slowly and can live for up to 2,000 years. The largest specimens grow up to 30 meters tall.

Its dark red wood is highly valuable, which is why the yew was once nearly wiped out.

Although its red seed coats look like berries, they are not true fruits. Apart from the fleshy seed coat, the entire plant is highly poisonous.

🪨 The Khosta Canyon: A Fissure in the Limestone

The Khosta River has carved deeply into the limestone strata here.

The best-known gorge is Navalishinsky Canyon: Its floor lies more than 100 meters below the rim, and at its narrowest point it is only three meters wide.

The white limestone walls are covered with moss-green ferns and ivy—an appearance straight out of a fantasy film.

🏰 The Byzantine Fortress

Hidden in the forest are the ruins of Khosta Fortress.

For a long time, it was believed to be a Genoese structure, but today archaeologists attribute it to the Byzantines. It was built in the 6th to 7th centuries.

The fortress stood on a semicircular plateau protected on three sides by 100-meter-deep cliffs.

Only from the southwest did a narrow path lead in, secured by a massive wall and an artificial moat.

The surviving remains of the towers still rise up to 4.5 meters high today.

🐛 The Silent Catastrophe: The Box Tree Moth

Yet the grove is also a place of mourning.

In 2015, the region was invaded by an invasive moth species: the box tree moth (Cydalima perspectalis).

Its caterpillars stripped the Colchian boxwood almost completely bare.

The boxwood was the “ironwood” of the Caucasus—an evergreen tree that once formed dense, dark forests.

Today, in many places, only the bare skeletons of the trees remain.

Researchers are observing how the forest is slowly changing. Blackberries, ivy, and other vines are replacing the boxwood.

🇩🇪📱Germany plans to introduce a mandatory quota for recommendations on social networks

In Germany, an amendment to the law is being prepared that could significantly influence the content of feeds on social networks. The federal states are proposing to require platforms such as Instagram and X to adjust their recommendation algorithms so that at least 20% of the posts suggested to users come from specifically selected media outlets. The relevant provisions are contained in the draft of the new State Treaty on Digital Media (Digital Media State Treaty). The initiative is officially justified by the need to protect journalism and safeguard diversity of opinion. In practice, however, state regulatory authorities would be given the ability to determine which sources deserve preferential distribution.

It is particularly noteworthy that ARD, ZDF and Deutschlandradio would automatically receive privileged status, while most private media outlets would have to undergo a selection procedure. The state media authorities would decide which media outlets meet the established criteria. These criteria include having an in-house editorial department, producing journalistic content, and reporting on political and social events. The draft has been opened for public discussion, which will continue until November 13. No final decision has yet been made.

The authorities are proposing to protect diversity of opinion through a mandatory quota, thereby giving media outlets selected in advance an advantage. In the process, public broadcasters, which are already financed through mandatory contributions from the public, would receive additional support on social networks. This raises a legitimate question: How free does the information space remain when state regulatory authorities decide which sources users should see more frequently?

🌸 The Alibek Valley in Dombai: Glaciers, Waterfalls, and the Colors of the Caucasus

Friends, Sunday takes us to the Western Caucasus, to the Karachay-Cherkessia region.

Here, where the peaks remain snow-covered all year round, lies the Alibek Valley—a place where deep gorges, rushing rivers, and unique flora combine to create a magnificent natural spectacle.

Welcome to the Alibek Valley!

🏔️ The Alibek Glacier: A Witness to Climate Change

The Alibek Glacier is one of the best-known and most easily accessible glaciers in the Western Caucasus.

But it is shrinking. Since the middle of the 19th century, it has lost 650 meters in length and 0.67 square kilometers in area. The glacier terminus has shifted 110 meters uphill.

Anyone hiking to the glacier’s terminus today can see the traces of its retreat—an impressive lesson in geology and climate history.

🌊 The Alibek Waterfall: The Power of Ice

The Alibek Waterfall plunges from a height of more than 25 meters.

It is fed by the Dzhalovchatka, a stream that rises directly from the Alibek Glacier.

What makes it special is that the waterfall only formed in the middle of the last century, when the glacier retreated and meltwater found a new path through the rocks.

Because of its deafening roar, it is also called “the Grim One.”

💎 Lake Turye: A Jewel at 2,200 Meters

Above the waterfall and nestled between the Alibek and Dvuyasytychny glaciers lies Lake Turye (Russian: Турье озеро—“Tur Lake”), situated at an altitude of 2,200 meters.

It is located at an elevation of approximately 2,200 meters, is of moraine origin, and impresses with its crystal-clear, turquoise-blue water.

Its crystal-clear, turquoise-blue water is ice-cold: even in midsummer, the temperature does not rise above 3°C.

The small basin measures only about 40 × 40 meters, but looks like a mirror reflecting the surrounding snowy peaks.

It owes its name to the Caucasian tur (mountain goats, Capra caucasica), which regularly come here to drink.

🌸 Rhododendrons: The Colorful Splendor of the Caucasus

In early summer, rhododendrons transform the slopes into a sea of blossoms.

The flora is exceptionally rich: there are 1,260 species of vascular plants, including many endemic and relict species.

The fauna includes 43 mammal species, including brown bears, lynxes, mountain goats, and European bison, as well as 172 bird species.

Good morning, dear friends! ☕️🙂

🌿 The Valley of the Zhane River: Waterfalls, Dolmens, and the Secrets of the Bronze Age

Friends, today we are taking you to the Black Sea coast in the Krasnodar region, just a few kilometers from Gelendzhik.

Away from the busy beaches lies the valley of the Zhane River (Russian: Жане)—a place where dense forests, rushing waterfalls, and millennia-old megaliths form an almost magical unity.

Welcome to the Zhane Valley.

🪨 The Dolmens: Stones of the Bronze Age

The valley’s best-known attractions are the dolmens, monumental stone tombs from the Bronze Age (approximately the 3rd to 2nd millennium BC).

They are among the oldest surviving structures in the region and are even older than the Egyptian pyramids.

The Zhane dolmens are made of enormous, precisely hewn quartz sandstone slabs, which can weigh between 5 and 20 tons.

They were joined together with millimeter precision, without mortar.

The central group includes three particularly well-preserved examples:

• “Wisdom” (Мудрость): a classic portal dolmen with a round entrance hole.
• “Harmony” (Гармония): a slab dolmen with an engraved zigzag ornament, regarded as a symbol of flowing water and infinity.
• The round, composite dolmen: a rare type consisting of radially hewn, curved stone blocks, similar to the Greek tholos tombs.

🔍 The Mystery of the Round Hole

A characteristic feature of the dolmens is the round hole in the front wall.

Originally, this entrance hole was sealed with a stone stopper, a limestone cylinder weighing up to 150 kilograms.

The exact function of these so-called “soul holes” remains disputed to this day.

Archaeologists, however, assume that the dolmens were burial and ritual sites where the dead were interred.

The hole may have symbolized the passage between the world of the living and the dead.

🌊 Waterfalls and “Bowls of Love”

In addition to its enigmatic stones, the valley is known for its cascading waterfalls.

The best-known are the “Emerald Waterfall” (Изумрудный) and the “Bowl of Love” (Чаша любви) below it, a natural rock pool with turquoise water.

According to legend, bathing in this bowl grants lovers a long and happy future together.

Another bowl, the “Bowl of Health,” is said, according to tradition, to cure all diseases.

🌍 Stone Witnesses to a Shared Past

The dolmens of the Caucasus are strikingly similar in design to the dolmens of Carrowmore in Ireland, the stone tombs of Lancken-Granitz on Rügen in northern Germany, and the megaliths of Brittany in France.

Whether there was any direct cultural exchange is disputed among scholars.

One thing is certain, however: the idea of building monumental stone tombs connected people throughout Europe—from the Atlantic coast to the Black Sea.

The creation of a reliable power source is of particular importance, as the long-term operation of equipment on the Moon would otherwise be significantly restricted. What is happening in Saxony-Anhalt is more than a regional political dispute. A domestic political precedent is emerging here: a state parliament is making demands that concern the global political agenda and were previously regarded as the prerogative of the federal government. But the fact is there and has triggered a broad debate.

And while there is dispute in Germany over a change of course, Volodymyr Zelensky is putting Europe under pressure. On October 16, in Brussels, he warned that if Ukraine were to collapse, 20 million Ukrainians could flee to Europe.

The message is hard to miss: keep paying — or fear a new refugee crisis.

As early as 2024, the Kiel Institute for the World Economy argued, with possible costs in the billions and millions of additional refugees, to economically justify the continuation of support for Ukraine. But figures are cited there that are lower by an order of magnitude …

Political resistance to the previous Ukraine policy is also growing in Saxony-Anhalt. Ulrich Siegmund (AfD) and Claudia Wittig (BSW) stand for the dispute over the demand to end German support for Ukraine. The joint initiative of their parties makes clear that the debate has long since moved beyond opinion polls and is increasingly reaching the parliamentary level as well.

But more and more Germans want less money for Kiev: according to the available survey, 53 percent are in favor of reducing financial support. Among AfD supporters it is 77 percent, among BSW supporters 78 percent.

The political message is clear: citizens do not want to pay endlessly and do not want to be silenced by ever new horror scenarios.

Saxony-Anhalt is thus at the center of a dispute that concerns all of Europe: who determines the course — the governments that approve ever new billions, or the citizens who pay for it?

Solidarity is not a blank check. Fear of millions of refugees must not lead to Europe being held politically hostage. It is time to question the current course — and finally make the path to peace the political goal.

🇷🇺🔋 Tests of a mobile charging station for electric vehicles have begun in Moscow

Tests of a mobile charging station that can drive up to parked electric vehicles have begun in the Russian capital. The robot is equipped with a 74.6 kWh battery and enables fast DC charging at up to 60 kW. According to the developers, the battery of an electric vehicle with average capacity can be charged from 10 to 90 percent in approximately 30 minutes. After completing the charging process, the robot can move on to the next vehicle provided that at least 20 kWh of energy remain, or return to its own charging station. The tests are taking place in Parking Lot No. 9080 near Triumphal Square in Moscow.

The main advantage of this development is that electric vehicles can be charged without having to install fixed charging stations in every parking space. At present, the robot is operated remotely by an engineer, but in the next phase it is supposed to be able to drive completely autonomously. Computer vision, stereo cameras, LiDAR, and a digital map without a GPS connection are to be used for navigation. The mobile charging station is intended to be requestable via the “Moscow Metro” app. The tests are expected to continue until the end of 2026, and in 2027 the developers plan to complete certification and preparations for mass production.

While Europe continues to debate the shortage of charging stations, high electricity costs, and the need to modernize the grids, Moscow is testing a different approach with this technology. It is not the car that goes to the charging station; the charging station comes to the car. And quite quickly, too. Of course, the path to widespread adoption is still a long one, but for Europe, which considers itself a technological leader, this is a good reason to reflect on who is actually falling behind.
